text: Card's college-proximity paper is NBER Working Paper 4483 (October 1993); Card (2000) lists its published version as a 1995 chapter in Aspects of Labour Market Behaviour: Essays in Honour of John Vanderkamp (University of Toronto Press), pp. 201-222. NBER Working Paper 4832 (August 1994) is a different paper, 'Earnings, Schooling, and Ability Revisited'.

Card's data are a 1976 cross-section of the National Longitudinal Survey of Young Men, which began in 1966 with men aged 14-24; the public extract nls.dat has 3,613 men interviewed in 1976 with valid education, of whom 3,010 report a valid 1976 wage (Card 1993, pp. 3-7 and Table 1).
The instrument is an indicator for an accredited four-year college in the respondent's local labor market in 1966, defined from county of residence in 1966 (Card 1993, p. 5 and fn. 7).
Card measures potential experience as age minus years of education minus six and includes it as a quadratic (Card 1993, p. 7).

All of Card's models include a Black indicator, indicators for southern and SMSA residence in 1976, eight indicators for region of residence in 1966, an indicator for SMSA residence in 1966, and experience and its square; the family-background set adds 14 variables: mother's and father's years of education, indicators for imputed (missing) parental education, eight indicators of parental-education classes, and two indicators of family structure at age 14 (Card 1993, Tables 2-4 notes).
Card's wage sample includes only wages between $1 and $30 per hour and excludes 49 observations with a missing 1966 interview month (Kling 2001, Table 1 note).
In Card's basic specification the OLS return to a year of schooling is 0.073 (standard error 0.004), N = 3,010 (Card 1993, Table 2 column 5; Table 4 row 1).
In Card's basic specification, growing up near a four-year college raises completed education by 0.365 years (standard error 0.105) (Card 1993, Table 3 Panel B column 2).
In Card's basic specification, growing up near a four-year college raises log hourly wages in 1976 by 0.048 (standard error 0.019) (Card 1993, Table 3 Panel B column 4).

Card's basic instrumental-variables estimate of the return to schooling is 0.132 (standard error 0.049), N = 3,010, with experience and its square treated as endogenous and instrumented by age and age squared (Card 1993, Table 3 Panel B column 6; Table 4 row 1).

With experience treated as exogenous, Card's IV estimates are 0.132 (0.055) without and 0.140 (0.055) with family-background controls; the corresponding first-stage coefficients on college proximity are 0.320 (0.088) and 0.322 (0.083) (Card 1993, Table 3 Panel A).
Card notes that the IV estimates are imprecise and that one cannot reject that the gap between the IV and OLS estimates is due to sampling error (Card 1993, p. 13 and fn. 17).

In models that treat experience as endogenous (instrumented by age and age squared), include the 14 family-background variables, enter college proximity directly in the earnings equation, and instrument education with proximity interacted with low parental education, Card's estimate of the direct effect of proximity on log wages is 0.015 (0.029); with proximity interacted with eight parental-education classes it is 0.013 (0.024) (Card 1993, Table 5, columns 3-4).
Kling (2001) replicated Card's estimates exactly: OLS 0.073 and IV 0.132 (0.049) for N = 3,010.

Blandhol, Bonney, Mogstad and Torgovitsky reproduce Card's IV estimate for Table 3 Panel A column 5 (experience exogenous, no family-background controls) with heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors (0.132, SE 0.054). They show that TSLS with additive (non-saturated) covariates has a weakly causal, LATE-type interpretation only under a 'rich covariates' condition; their RESET test rejects that condition for this specification (p = 0.000), and their estimates of LATE/ACR-type parameters are 0.067 (DDML) and 0.085 (IPSW).

Bi, Kang and Taylor report first-stage F statistics of 13.3 and 15.1 for Card's Table 3 Panel A specifications and find that, after conditioning on passing an F > 10 pre-test, the TSLS estimates are no longer significant at 5%.

With a reduced control set (experience, its square, Black, South, SMSA), Kang, Jiang, Zhao and Small report a first-stage F of 16.7 and an Anderson-Rubin 95% confidence interval of [0.038, 0.261] for the return to schooling in Card's data, computed under the package's default homoskedastic model.

As reported by Carr and Kitagawa (2021), tests of the testable implications of instrument validity, with education binarised at 16 or more years, reject Card's college-proximity instrument without covariates (Kitagawa 2015) but not when conditioning on Card's full covariate set (Carr and Kitagawa 2021); Carr and Kitagawa note that binarising the treatment can itself violate the exclusion restriction through coarsening bias.
For one endogenous regressor and one instrument, the Stock-Yogo critical value for the first-stage F at a 10% maximal size of a nominal 5% Wald test is 16.38, derived under homoskedastic errors.

The Montiel Olea-Pflueger effective F is robust to heteroskedasticity, autocorrelation and clustering, equals the robust first-stage F when the model is just identified, and its simplified 5% critical value for a 10% worst-case bias threshold with one instrument is 23.1.

Andrews, Stock and Sun recommend judging instrument strength by the effective F and, with a single instrument, reporting identification-robust Anderson-Rubin confidence sets whatever the first-stage F, because these are efficient regardless of instrument strength.

The Anderson-Rubin test inverts the restriction that the reduced-form coefficient equals the first-stage coefficient times the structural coefficient; its heteroskedasticity-robust version has a chi-squared null distribution regardless of instrument strength.
In the single-instrument model a valid 5% t-test requires a first-stage F above 104.7; keeping a threshold of 10 requires a critical value of 3.43 instead of 1.96.

Conley, Hansen and Rossi relax the exclusion restriction by letting the instrument have a direct effect gamma on the outcome; given only a support for gamma, the union over that support of the gamma-specific 2SLS confidence intervals has asymptotic coverage of at least the nominal level.
The Stata command plausexog implements the Conley-Hansen-Rossi bounds.

In Card's specification that treats experience as exogenous and includes the family-background controls, the IV return to schooling is 0.140 (0.055), the first-stage coefficient on college proximity is 0.322 (0.083) and the reduced-form coefficient on log wages is 0.045 (0.018) (Card 1993, Table 3 Panel A columns 6, 2 and 4); the OLS estimate with the same controls is 0.073 (0.004) (Table 2 column 5).
Without family-background controls, Card's OLS return is 0.075 (0.003) (Card 1993, Table 2 column 2).

On Card's data with controls for experience and its square, race, South, SMSA, region in 1966 and SMSA in 1966 (Card's Table 3 Panel A column 5), Cinelli and Hazlett report an IV estimate of 0.132 with an Anderson-Rubin 95% confidence interval of [0.025, 0.285] and a t-value of 2.33 against a zero effect.

Cinelli and Hazlett find that omitted variables explaining 0.67% of the residual variation of both proximity and log earnings (robustness value), or 0.05% of the residual variation of proximity with no limit on the outcome side (extreme robustness value), suffice to make Card's IV estimate statistically insignificant; their framework treats violations of the exclusion restriction and confounding of the instrument with the same tools.

According to Cinelli and Hazlett, omitted variables as strong as the SMSA indicator or the Black indicator could widen the Anderson-Rubin interval for Card's return to schooling to about [-0.02, 0.40].

Steiner, Houssineau and Steel allow college proximity a direct effect on log wages between 0 and a and find that positive returns to schooling in Card's data are robust to a direct effect of 1% but not to 2% or 4%, with the lower probability of a positive return falling to 0.887, 0.748 and 0.517 for a = 0.02, 0.03 and 0.04.

For an over-identified version of Card's model (education, experience and its square endogenous; public, private and two-year college proximity, age and age squared as instruments; family background, region and race as controls), Londschien reports a TSLS estimate of 0.145, a LIML estimate of 0.172 and a subvector Anderson-Rubin 95% confidence set of [0.083, 0.352] for the return to schooling.

Delbianco reproduces Card's Table 3 Panel A column 5 (first stage 0.320, first-stage F 13.3, IV 0.132 (0.055)) and finds that a fourth-cumulant test of the exclusion restriction is uninformative in these data.

Słoczyński, Uysal and Wooldridge reanalyse Card's data with binarised schooling (some college; college completion) and obtain 2SLS estimates of 0.661 (0.294) and 1.392 (0.798), which they regard as implausibly large given possible failures of exclusion and monotonicity.

In Kling's model, with college proximity independent of the relevant unobservables conditional on the covariates X and with monotonicity, the 2SLS schooling coefficient is a weighted average of the heterogeneous marginal benefits of schooling for those whose schooling choice is affected by the instrument, conditional on X (Kling 2001, NBER WP p. 4).

Angrist and Imbens show that, given mild regularity assumptions, instrumental-variables independence assumptions identify a weighted average of per-unit causal effects along the causal response function for a variable treatment such as years of schooling, and that conventional IV and 2SLS can be interpreted as estimating this average causal response (abstract of the 1992 NBER version; the abstract names no monotonicity, covariate or complier condition).

On Card's data with a binary treatment, schooling of more than 12 years ('some college'), and Card's covariates without family background (n = 2,988), so for a different estimand from Card's per-year return, Tübbicke finds a 2SLS estimate of the return to college of 0.603 (0.289), against 0.279-0.323 from instrument-propensity-score matching and weighting estimators, and attributes the 50-100% gap to the conditional-variance weighting implicit in linear-in-covariates 2SLS. Reporting Słoczyński (2021), who attributes the large 2SLS estimate to defiers, he also shows that a reordered instrument that accounts for defiers lowers the saturated-specification 2SLS estimate from 0.570 to 0.289.

Card's own later survey reports the proximity estimates of his 1995 chapter as OLS 0.073 (0.004), IV 0.132 (0.049), and 0.097 (0.048) with proximity interacted with family background as the instrument (Card 2000, Table 2 row 4), the same values as NBER WP 4483.

Two principal-stratification reanalyses of Card's NLS Young Men data drop the exclusion restriction and use a binary intermediate variable, schooling beyond high school (Jiang, Yang and Ding 2022; Luo, Li, Miao and He 2024). In their preferred specifications they find no significant direct effect of college proximity on log wages for always-takers or never-takers. Their complier effects are imprecise and not on Card's per-year scale: Jiang et al.'s triply robust estimate is 0.10 (95% interval -0.01 to 0.23), and Luo et al.'s preferred estimate is 0.85 (0.00 to 1.88) log points. One of Luo et al.'s outcome-model specifications that omit the IQ proxy, which the authors regard as misspecified, gives a significantly negative never-taker effect of -0.86 (-2.83 to -0.32), which would be a direct effect of proximity.

Under conditional homoskedasticity, the subvector Anderson-Rubin test that replaces the untested coefficients by their LIML estimates and uses chi-square critical values with k - m_W degrees of freedom (k instruments, m_W untested endogenous coefficients) has correct asymptotic size without assumptions on the strength of identification; the corresponding subvector LM test is size-distorted.

Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2019) show that the homoskedastic subvector AR test with chi-square(k - m_W) critical values is conservative and inadmissible, and propose data-dependent critical values that depend on the largest root of the subvector AR characteristic polynomial, a measure of how strongly the untested coefficients are identified; for k - m_W = 1 at the 5% level these critical values rise from 0.4 to 3.838 as that statistic rises from 0.5 to 1000, against the chi-square(1) value of 3.841.

Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis state that their subvector AR analysis relies critically on homoskedasticity, and that both their conditional test and the chi-square(k - m_W) subvector AR test must have asymptotic size above the nominal level under arbitrary heteroskedasticity.

The projection method forms a subvector confidence set from a confidence set for the full coefficient vector; with the AR statistic this means minimising AR over the nuisance coefficients and comparing the minimum with the chi-square(k) critical value of the full-vector test, which gives sets that are often conservative. The reduced-degrees-of-freedom result of Guggenberger et al. (2012) is for homoskedastic errors and, according to Andrews, Stock and Sun, does not extend to the general non-homoskedastic case.

Guggenberger, Kleibergen and Mavroeidis (2024) propose a subvector AR test valid under arbitrary conditional heteroskedasticity: it adapts their 2019 conditional test when a covariance matrix is approximately of Kronecker-product form, as decided by a model-selection step, and otherwise uses Andrews's (2017) heteroskedasticity-robust AR/AR test; its asymptotic size is bounded by the nominal size.

The Python package ivmodels implements the subvector Anderson-Rubin test with chi-square(k - m_W), F, or Guggenberger-Kleibergen-Mavroeidis (2019) critical values and its inversion into confidence sets; it has no heteroskedasticity-robust option, and its authors state that their results do not allow for general heteroskedasticity.

The Stata command twostepweakiv provides heteroskedasticity-, autocorrelation- and cluster-robust weak-instrument-robust confidence sets and, through its project() option, confidence sets for one endogenous coefficient that treat the other endogenous coefficients as nuisance parameters, using the refined projection method of Chaudhuri and Zivot (2011) with K or linear-combination tests.

Replicated 2SLS coefficient on years of schooling in Card's basic specification (WP 4483 Table 3 Panel B column 6: schooling, experience and its square endogenous, instrumented by college proximity, age and age squared; base and family-background controls), N = 3,010 men with a 1976 wage, NLS Young Men, unweighted (published 0.132; reproduced). It is the coefficient on schooling in this linear model, not the average return for all men. Under monotonicity and a correctly specified (rich) covariate adjustment a 2SLS coefficient would be, conditional on the covariates, a positively weighted average of returns for men whose schooling responds to proximity, but both conditions are in doubt: Blandhol et al. reject rich covariates for Panel A column 5, and Tubbicke, for a different estimand (a binary some-college treatment without family-background controls, n = 2,988), finds 2SLS well above estimators that do not rely on them and, reporting Sloczynski, that allowing for defiers roughly halves 2SLS; so even that reading is not guaranteed here. Because experience and its square are also instrumented (by age), those complier results do not directly define whose return this coefficient weights.

Largest characteristic root kappa_1 of the homoskedastic subvector AR problem at the Panel B column 6 2SLS estimate, the conditioning statistic of the GKM19 critical value (which approaches the chi-square(1) value as kappa_1 grows). With two nuisance regressors it reflects only the best-identified direction of the (Y0, W) system, so it does not show that experience and its square are separately well identified; and it changes with the hypothesised b0, because experience plus schooling equals age minus 6, which lies in the instruments' span.

Report-only, descriptive and post hoc: the homoskedastic subvector AR statistic kappa_p at a zero return to schooling in Card's basic specification, on the chi-square scale (GKMC rejects above 3.841, and kappa_p equals 3.841 at the GKMC bounds). Next to the robust projection statistic at zero (b6-rob-m-at-zero, compared with chi-square(3) = 7.815) it is not larger, so the robust and homoskedastic sets differ on zero through their critical values (chi-square(3) for the projection, chi-square(1) or GKM19 for the homoskedastic tests), not through a smaller robust statistic. This changes neither the H3(b) decision rule nor its primary set: the robust projection set decides, and it contains zero.
